AvioHMI AvioHMI is a mission computer and ground-control suite that flies a fleet of aircraft — either a 3-aircraft simulation or **real ADS-B traffic pulled live from the OpenSky Network** — and streams position, speed, heading, attitude, and fuel state over WebSocket to a web-based ground-control dashboard, a touch-screen cockpit display, and both AR (phone camera + compass) and VR (WebXR) 3D views, while an ffmpeg → CUDA pipeline decodes a real sensor video and feeds GPU-accelerated Sobel edge detection into a live HUD overlay [2]. Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Core["Mission Computer Core (Java)"] SIM["SensorSimulator × 3 AVIO101 / 102 / 103"] WS["WebSocketServer :8765"] HTTPSRV["TelemetryHttpServer :8766"] REPO["TelemetryRepository"] HUDT["HUD overlay thread"] SIM --> WS SIM --> REPO HUDT --> HTTPSRV end FFMPEG["ffmpeg decodes sample_sensor_feed.mp4"] CUDA["video-processing (C++/CUDA) Sobel + HUD compositing called via JNI, subprocess fallback"] PG[("PostgreSQL / PostGIS")] GC["Ground Control (React)"] MFD["Cockpit MFD (Flutter)"] HUDT -- "extract current frame" --> FFMPEG FFMPEG -- "current_frame.pgm" --> HUDT HUDT -- "heading / speed / altitude + frame" --> CUDA CUDA -- "live_overlay.bmp" --> HUDT REPO <--> PG [1].

That overlay comes from a real pipeline: every few seconds Core shells out to `ffmpeg` to decode the current frame of `video-processing/assets/sample_sensor_feed.mp4` into a PGM, then hands that frame to `video-processing/edge_detect.exe`, which runs it through the CUDA Sobel kernel and composites the lead aircraft's live heading/speed/altitude into the HUD [5]. Features The pipeline itself is proper C++ (RAII image classes, a `SobelProcessor` owning its own device-memory lifetime) called **in-process from Java via JNI** (`video-processing/hud_native.dll`) rather than shelled out to per frame — falling back to spawning `edge_detect.exe` as a subprocess if the native library wasn't built for the platform [1].

- **Live alerts** — overspeed, off-course (cross-track distance from the planned route), and low-fuel warnings computed from real telemetry and surfaced as a banner [1]. - **History playback** — telemetry is persisted to PostgreSQL/PostGIS; a scrubber lets you rewind and replay any aircraft's recorded flight [1].

![Temperature and axial thermal stress in the blade section](docs/img/blade_results.png) The solver is written from scratch on top of Eigen's sparse matrices: element routines, assembly, boundary conditions, a Gmsh mesh reader and HDF5/XDMF output [2]. Centrifugal and gas-bending loads, which dominate real blade stresses together with thermal ones, are not included [5].
Kaynaklarda bu soruya yanıt bulamadım.

Hot gas heats the outer surface, cooling air flows through internal passages, and the resulting temperature field loads a structural model of the section [3]. **These inputs are illustrative.** The film coefficients are assumed rather than computed from the flow, and the section is not a real engine blade [1].

The Catch2 suite (30 scenarios, written `SCENARIO / GIVEN / WHEN / THEN`) adds checks that must hold exactly, not just converge: - patch tests on distorted meshes; - uniaxial tension, and free and fully clamped thermal expansion; - heat balance across all boundaries to round-off; - self-equilibrated thermal loads that leave statically determinate supports unloaded; - error handling for ill-posed problems and malformed inputs [1].
- **At-least-once delivery handled explicitly.** SQS can deliver a message twice; the analyzer skips jobs that are already `DONE` so a paid LLM call is never repeated [1].

It's built around a question every fielded perception system has to answer honestly: **not "does it run," but "how well does it actually work, and how do you know?"** - **Full geometric CV + real-time systems pipeline in C++17** — stereo calibration/rectification, BM/SGBM disparity, metric depth, 3D reprojection, ONNX detection, Kalman-filter 3D multi-object tracking, and monocular-with-stereo-scale visual odometry — not a single stage, the whole chain [4].

AvioHMI AvioHMI is a mission computer and ground-control suite that flies a fleet of aircraft — either a 3-aircraft simulation or **real ADS-B traffic pulled live from the OpenSky Network** — and streams position, speed, heading, attitude, and fuel state over WebSocket to a web-based ground-control dashboard, a touch-screen cockpit display, and both AR (phone camera + compass) and VR (WebXR) 3D views, while an ffmpeg → CUDA pipeline decodes a real sensor video and feeds GPU-accelerated Sobel edge detection into a live HUD overlay [2]. Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Core["Mission Computer Core (Java)"] SIM["SensorSimulator × 3 AVIO101 / 102 / 103"] WS["WebSocketServer :8765"] HTTPSRV["TelemetryHttpServer :8766"] REPO["TelemetryRepository"] HUDT["HUD overlay thread"] SIM --> WS SIM --> REPO HUDT --> HTTPSRV end FFMPEG["ffmpeg decodes sample_sensor_feed.mp4"] CUDA["video-processing (C++/CUDA) Sobel + HUD compositing called via JNI, subprocess fallback"] PG[("PostgreSQL / PostGIS")] GC["Ground Control (React)"] MFD["Cockpit MFD (Flutter)"] HUDT -- "extract current frame" --> FFMPEG FFMPEG -- "current_frame.pgm" --> HUDT HUDT -- "heading / speed / altitude + frame" --> CUDA CUDA -- "live_overlay.bmp" --> HUDT REPO <--> PG [1].

That overlay comes from a real pipeline: every few seconds Core shells out to `ffmpeg` to decode the current frame of `video-processing/assets/sample_sensor_feed.mp4` into a PGM, then hands that frame to `video-processing/edge_detect.exe`, which runs it through the CUDA Sobel kernel and composites the lead aircraft's live heading/speed/altitude into the HUD [5]. Features The pipeline itself is proper C++ (RAII image classes, a `SobelProcessor` owning its own device-memory lifetime) called **in-process from Java via JNI** (`video-processing/hud_native.dll`) rather than shelled out to per frame — falling back to spawning `edge_detect.exe` as a subprocess if the native library wasn't built for the platform [1].

- **Live alerts** — overspeed, off-course (cross-track distance from the planned route), and low-fuel warnings computed from real telemetry and surfaced as a banner [1]. - **History playback** — telemetry is persisted to PostgreSQL/PostGIS; a scrubber lets you rewind and replay any aircraft's recorded flight [1].

![Temperature and axial thermal stress in the blade section](docs/img/blade_results.png) The solver is written from scratch on top of Eigen's sparse matrices: element routines, assembly, boundary conditions, a Gmsh mesh reader and HDF5/XDMF output [2]. Centrifugal and gas-bending loads, which dominate real blade stresses together with thermal ones, are not included [5].
Kaynaklarda bu soruya yanıt bulamadım.

Hot gas heats the outer surface, cooling air flows through internal passages, and the resulting temperature field loads a structural model of the section [3]. **These inputs are illustrative.** The film coefficients are assumed rather than computed from the flow, and the section is not a real engine blade [1].

The Catch2 suite (30 scenarios, written `SCENARIO / GIVEN / WHEN / THEN`) adds checks that must hold exactly, not just converge: - patch tests on distorted meshes; - uniaxial tension, and free and fully clamped thermal expansion; - heat balance across all boundaries to round-off; - self-equilibrated thermal loads that leave statically determinate supports unloaded; - error handling for ill-posed problems and malformed inputs [1].
- **At-least-once delivery handled explicitly.** SQS can deliver a message twice; the analyzer skips jobs that are already `DONE` so a paid LLM call is never repeated [1].
